MANCHESTER SCHOOL DISTRICT SAU #37 
COMMITTEE ON TEACHING AND LEARNING 
 
October 27, 2026 6:00 p.m. 
 
1. Chair Parr called the meeting to order at 6:05 p.m. 
 
2. The Clerk called the roll. 
 
Present: Committee Members Parr, Turner, Stewart, Georges, Smith and Student Members 
Lual and Gammella. 
 
3. Public Forum  
 
There was no one present wishing to give comment during public forum. 
 
4. Approval of Minutes from the September 22, 2026, Teaching and Learning Committee Meeting 
 
On motion of Committee Member Turner, duly seconded by Committee Member Stewart, it was moved 
to approve the minutes of the September 22, 2026 Teaching and Learning meeting.  All were in favor and 
the motion passed. 
 
5.         Presentations    
 
a. Jewett Street Elementary School - School Report Card Presentation  – by Peter Lubelczyk, 
Principal of Jewett Street Elementary School 
 
Principal Peter Lubelczyk and Assistant Principal Pam Agate presented Jewett Street Elementary School's 
Attendance, Behavior, and Curriculum (ABC) goals for the 2026–2027 school year.  He thanked the 
Committee for the opportunity to highlight the school's accomplishments, current initiatives, and goals for 
the academic year.  He explained that Jewett Street places a strong emphasis on recognizing student 
achievement, not only academically but also through positive behavior, social-emotional growth, and 
meaningful engagement in learning. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk discussed the school's implementation of the Multi-Tiered System of Supports for 
Behavior (MTSS-B), noting that the program has had a significant positive impact on school culture. 
The school has established common behavioral expectations focused on being respectful, responsible, and 
safe. 
 Each month, staff members nominate students who demonstrate excellence in one or more of these 
areas.

 Recognized students are celebrated during a school-wide assembly and receive certificates and 
acknowledgment from their peers and staff. 
 Families receive an email containing a photograph of their child and an explanation of the 
accomplishment for which the student was recognized. 
 Principal Lubelczyk reported that the response from students and families has been extremely 
positive and that the celebrations reinforce the school's shared expectations. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk also highlighted students' engagement in academic learning, including their 
participation in i-Ready assessments and instructional activities early in the school year.  He explained 
that Jewett Street's work aligns with the District's strategic priorities of growing learners, educators, and 
systems.  The school's overarching goal is to establish strong academic foundations, develop critical 
thinking and problem-solving skills, nurture social-emotional growth, and prepare students to become 
engaged citizens and lifelong learners. 
 
Attendance Goal 
 
Principal Lubelczyk reported that the school's attendance goal focuses on a specific cohort of students 
who experienced chronic absenteeism during the 2025–2026 school year.  The cohort consists of students 
who accumulated 20 or more absences during the previous academic year.  The school's goal is to reduce 
the total number of absences for these students by 25% during the 2026–2027 school year. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk emphasized that improving attendance requires a collaborative effort involving 
students, families, classroom teachers, administration, guidance staff, and the school social worker. 
The school is implementing several strategies to support improved attendance: 
 Establishing individualized attendance success plans for identified students. 
 Implementing Check and Connect mentoring and maintaining regular communication with 
families. 
 Conducting weekly student check-ins involving classroom teachers, administrators, guidance 
personnel, and the school social worker. 
 Holding regular attendance meetings to review student progress, evaluate the effectiveness of 
intervention plans, and make necessary adjustments.
October 27, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 3 of 54 
 
 
 Recognizing improved attendance through postcards, telephone calls, text messages, and other 
positive communications with families. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk explained that these strategies are intended to identify barriers preventing students 
from attending school consistently and provide the support necessary to address those challenges.  He 
reported that the school was already beginning to observe encouraging results among students in the 
identified cohort.  Principal Lubelczyk specifically recognized Caroline Glennon, the school's new social 
worker, who also works with the preschool program at Bishop O'Neill.  He praised Ms. Glennon's ability 
to connect with students and families, build positive relationships, and bring individuals together to 
address attendance challenges. 
 
Behavior Goal 
 
Principal Lubelczyk explained that the school's behavior goal builds upon progress made during the 
previous academic year in strengthening Tier Two behavioral interventions.  He reported that Jewett 
Street developed several intervention strategies, including: 
 Check-In/Check-Out. 
 Small social groups. 
 Larger social groups. 
 Quiet lunch opportunities. 
 Individualized behavioral supports based on student needs. 
 
Approximately 45 to 50 students participated in these interventions during the previous school year. 
The school's MTSS-B Tier Two team met regularly to review individual student needs, identify 
appropriate interventions, and evaluate student progress.  For the 2026–2027 school year, the goal is to 
strengthen the monitoring process and establish a more fluid system that allows students to enter and exit 
Tier Two interventions based on their needs and demonstrated progress. 
 
Key actions include: 
 Developing a monitoring system for students who have completed interventions. 
 Holding weekly meetings to assess progress and determine when students are ready to exit 
specific supports.
October 27, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 4 of 54 
 
 
 Maintaining consistent communication with classroom teachers before and after students complete 
interventions. 
 Using student data to make decisions regarding continued participation, adjustments to 
interventions, or successful completion. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk explained that success would be demonstrated through measurable improvements in 
student behavior, students successfully completing interventions, and the ability to serve additional 
students as openings become available.  He reported that the school had already identified returning 
students who continued to require support and had begun serving newly identified students.  Some 
students who began interventions during the previous school year were demonstrating sufficient progress 
to be considered for completion of those supports.   
 
Principal Lubelczyk viewed this as an encouraging indication that the school's intervention systems were 
working effectively. 
 
Curriculum and Academic Goal 
 
Principal Lubelczyk reported that the school's academic goal is for 90% of students at each grade level to 
successfully meet their individualized literacy goals, established using beginning-of-year assessment data. 
He explained that the school is focused on strengthening Tier One literacy instruction through Amplify 
and the Being a Writer program, with reading and writing specialists providing modeling, coaching, and 
co-teaching.  Tier Two interventions will focus on specific literacy needs and provide individualized or 
small-group instruction to students requiring additional support. 
 
The school's instructional strategies and progress monitoring include: 
 Strengthening Tier One literacy instruction through modeling, coaching, and co-teaching. 
 Providing targeted Tier Two interventions designed to address individual literacy needs. 
 Conducting biweekly progress monitoring using mCLASS and DIBELS assessments. 
 Reviewing student data during Professional Learning Community (PLC) meetings. 
 Using midyear assessment results to evaluate student growth. 
 Closely monitoring students identified in the red and yellow performance categories to determine 
whether interventions are producing the intended results.
October 27, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 5 of 54 
 
 
 
Principal Lubelczyk highlighted an important development for the current school year: Jewett Street 
welcomed ten student interns from Southern New Hampshire University and Saint Anselm College. 
Two interns will be assigned to each grade level, kindergarten through fourth grade.  The interns will 
work with classroom teachers, multilingual learner teachers, special education teachers, and intervention 
staff to provide targeted small-group literacy support. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk explained that the additional assistance will significantly increase the number of 
students receiving individualized instruction while allowing intervention groups to remain flexible based 
on student progress.  The expanded support will also allow Reading Specialist Katie Howe to spend 
additional time working directly with classroom teachers through modeling and co-teaching.  He 
highlighted Ms. Howe's expertise in writing instruction and described the positive impact her work has 
had on student engagement. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk shared an example from fourth-grade teacher Angie Scora, who reported that 
students had become so enthusiastic about writing that they were disappointed when it was time to 
transition to another classroom activity.  He stated that this enthusiasm demonstrated the progress students 
were making and reflected the growing excitement surrounding literacy instruction. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk concluded by expressing pride in Jewett Street's students, families, and staff. 
He noted that the school had experienced improvements in state assessment results in both reading and 
writing but acknowledged that additional work remained.  He emphasized that academic growth, positive 
behavior, social-emotional development, and students' excitement about learning are all important 
measures of the school's success. 
 
Committee Members questions and comments included: 
1.  Committee Member Stewart thanked Principal Lubelczyk and Assistant Principal Agate 
for their presentation and congratulated the school on its reported 38% results in 
mathematics and English.  She described the school's goal of reducing chronic absenteeism 
by 25% as ambitious and asked whether the administration was confident in its ability to 
achieve that goal.

Assistant Principal Agate indicated that the school was already beginning to see positive results among 
students participating in the attendance interventions. 
 
2.  Committee Member Stewart asked Principal Lubelczyk to elaborate on the school's efforts 
to engage parents and guardians. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk emphasized that strong family involvement begins with Jewett Street's active Parent 
Teacher Association (PTA).  He explained that PTA members work diligently to organize events that 
bring families together and strengthen the school's sense of community.  He highlighted several strategies 
contributing to family engagement: 
 Maintaining an active PTA that organizes events and encourages family participation. 
 Using TalkingPoints to strengthen communication between teachers and families. 
 Sharing information regularly and transparently, including when difficult conversations are 
necessary. 
 Encouraging open communication so that families and staff can work collaboratively to address 
concerns. 
 Celebrating student accomplishments and providing opportunities for families to participate in 
school activities. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk stated that transparent communication has remained a priority throughout his years at 
Jewett Street.  He explained that maintaining open partnerships with families allows the school to address 
concerns, celebrate accomplishments, and support students more effectively.  He reported that the school's 
recent open house was one of the most heavily attended he could recall and expressed enthusiasm for 
upcoming family events. 
 
3.  Committee Member Stewart referenced the additional building space that Jewett Street is 
expected to receive and suggested that the expansion would further support the school's 
progress. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk expressed excitement about the additional space and the opportunities it would 
provide for the school.

Page 7 of 54 
 
 
4.  Committee Member Stewart asked whether having ten student interns was unusual and 
how the school had been able to secure such a substantial number. 
 
Assistant Principal Agate confirmed that ten interns represented a significant increase, noting that the 
school had only three interns during the previous year.  She explained that the experience with those 
interns had been extremely positive and that the school welcomed the opportunity to expand the 
partnership. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk also highlighted the school's relationship with Memorial High School, explaining that 
Memorial students frequently return to Jewett Street to volunteer.  Some students are interested in 
pursuing careers in education, while others are completing community service requirements or returning 
to support a school they previously attended.  He emphasized that these students serve as positive role 
models for younger children and may ultimately pursue careers in education. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk thanked Memorial High School staff and administrators, including Amy Christopher 
and Ben Dick, for supporting the partnership. 
 
5. Committee Member Stewart congratulated the school and encouraged the administration to 
continue its efforts. 
 
6.  Committee Member Turner thanked the presenters and highlighted two consistent themes 
throughout the presentation: celebration and communication.  She noted that recognizing 
positive attendance, behavior, and academic accomplishments helps students feel 
connected to their school and encourages them to participate more fully in their 
educational experiences.   
 
7. Committee Member Turner emphasized the importance of celebrating student successes, 
explaining that positive recognition can have a lasting effect on elementary students and 
contribute to a welcoming and supportive school environment. 
 
8. She also praised the school's commitment to communication with families and among 
teachers and support staff.  Committee Member Turner noted that effective communication

is particularly important when monitoring students participating in behavioral and 
academic interventions, including determining when students are ready to complete Tier 
Two supports.  She expressed enthusiasm for the expanded small-group literacy 
interventions and the additional individualized attention students would receive. 
 
9. Committee Member Turner also praised the school's efforts to create excitement around 
reading and writing. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk acknowledged the comments and recognized Chris Pelletier for providing UFLI 
training to the ten student interns.  He explained that the training would help prepare the interns to support 
literacy instruction and small-group interventions. 
 
Committee Member Turner acknowledged Ms. Pelletier's expertise and thanked the school for its 
continued work. 
 
10.  Committee Member Smith reflected on how substantially Jewett Street Elementary School 
had changed over the previous twenty years.  She noted that while the school was different 
from the one he remembered, he was impressed by the progress being made and the 
positive results students were experiencing. 
 
11. Committee Member Smith acknowledged that the school had undergone significant 
changes, including changes to the grade levels served, but emphasized that the 
administration and staff were clearly making a positive difference for students. She praised 
the school's leadership and staff for their dedication and expressed appreciation for the 
continued focus on student success. 
 
Principal Lubelczyk explained that Jewett Street continues to maintain a strong connection to its history 
and traditions.  He shared that he is a former Jewett Street student, as are Guidance Counselor Charles 
Vorias and Social Worker Caroline Glennon.
October 27, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 9 of 54 
 
 
Principal Lubelczyk stated that these connections help preserve the school's sense of community and the 
positive experiences associated with its history.  He explained that the administration and staff strive to 
maintain those traditions while continuing to improve educational opportunities for current students. 
 
12. Committee Member Smith expressed appreciation for the school's progress and 
encouraged the administration to continue its work. 
 
13. Chair Parr thanked Principal Lubelczyk and Assistant Principal Agate for their 
comprehensive presentation and their dedication to Jewett Street Elementary School.  He 
expressed appreciation for the positive work being undertaken to improve attendance, 
strengthen behavioral supports, increase literacy achievement, and promote meaningful 
engagement among students and families. 
 
b. BioTech: Road to the Future Presentation – by Mary Hartigan-Demers,    
Teacher at Hillside Middle School and Sophia Sheehan, Teacher at  
Manchester High School West 
 
Mary Hartigan-Demers, a teacher at Hillside Middle School, and Sophia Sheehan, a teacher at Manchester 
High School West, presented information regarding their participation in Manchester Creates and the 
opportunities being developed to expand biotechnology, biofabrication, and regenerative medicine 
education throughout the Manchester School District. 
 
Assistant Superintendent Nicole Doherty introduced the presenters and praised their commitment to 
expanding their professional knowledge and translating those experiences into meaningful project-based 
learning opportunities for students.  She emphasized that their work represents an exciting opportunity to 
connect classroom instruction with emerging science and technology industries in Manchester and 
throughout New Hampshire. 
 
Ms. Mary Hartigan-Demers, a teacher at Hillside Middle School, and Ms. Sophia Sheehan, a teacher at 
Manchester High School West, presented Biotechnology: Road to the Future, highlighting their 
participation in Manchester Creates and the opportunities being developed to expand biotechnology, 
biofabrication, and regenerative medicine education throughout the Manchester School District.
October 27, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 10 of 54 
 
 
The presenters discussed how their professional learning experiences have strengthened science 
instruction, increased student engagement, and created partnerships with colleges, universities, 
researchers, and biotechnology organizations. 
 
Manchester Creates and Professional Learning 
 
Ms. Sheehan explained that she and Ms. Hartigan-Demers participated in the first cohort of Manchester 
Creates, a grant-supported professional learning initiative designed to introduce educators to biomedical 
engineering, biofabrication, regenerative medicine, and related scientific concepts.  The program provided 
opportunities for educators to expand their scientific knowledge, collaborate with professionals in the 
field, and incorporate hands-on learning experiences into their classrooms. 
 
Ms. Sheehan highlighted several important benefits of the experience: 
 Renewed enthusiasm and passion for teaching science. 
 Increased confidence in presenting complex scientific concepts. 
 Stronger connections with community organizations, colleges, universities, and industry 
professionals. 
 Opportunities to connect classroom instruction with real-world scientific research. 
 Greater student engagement through project-based learning, experimentation, and problem-
solving. 
 Increased opportunities for students to develop critical thinking, collaboration, and communication 
skills. 
 
Ms. Sheehan explained that the program encouraged teachers to move beyond traditional classroom 
instruction and provide students with opportunities to develop their own ideas, design experiments, and 
explore scientific concepts through authentic research. 
 
Ms. Hartigan-Demers discussed how Manchester Creates strengthened collaboration between 
Manchester's middle and high schools, particularly across different areas of the City.  She noted that she 
was the only middle school teacher participating in the first cohort, which provided a valuable opportunity 
to work alongside high school educators and develop instructional connections across grade levels.
October 27, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 11 of 54 
 
 
Through the program, Ms. Hartigan-Demers developed classroom projects involving regenerative 
medicine and biofabrication, including experiments related to plant tissue regeneration and stem cell 
modeling.  She emphasized the importance of students recognizing that advanced scientific research and 
biotechnology development are taking place within their own community and that these fields may 
provide future educational and career opportunities. 
 
Biomedical Research and Student Participation 
 
The presenters discussed their participation in the New Hampshire IDeA Network of Biomedical 
Research Excellence (NH-INBRE), which connects academic institutions and research organizations to 
strengthen biomedical research and educational opportunities.  Ms. Hartigan-Demers explained that 
students at Hillside Middle School participated in experiments involving the decellularization and 
recellularization of spinach leaves.  She described how researchers are examining whether the vascular 
structures found in plants can be used as scaffolds for growing human tissue, including potential 
applications involving heart tissue. 
 
Ms. Hartigan-Demers reported that she and a former student, Liz Sheehan, presented their classroom 
research during a poster session at an NH-INBRE gathering. 
 Liz was an eighth-grade student at the time of the research. 
 She had the opportunity to present and explain the project to college professors and other scientific 
professionals. 
 The research involved examining the use of plant vascular structures in regenerative medicine. 
 Ms. Hartigan-Demers noted that researchers were impressed by Liz's ability to understand and 
communicate advanced scientific concepts at such a young age. 
 
Ms. Hartigan-Demers emphasized that this experience demonstrated the potential of project-based 
learning to build students' confidence and provide opportunities that extend well beyond the traditional 
classroom. 
 
Ms. Sheehan also discussed the research-based activities she has developed for her high school biology 
classes.  She explained that students use plants as models to explore how cells communicate, respond to
October 27, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 12 of 54 
 
 
damage, and regenerate tissue.  These activities allow students to make connections between plant 
biology, human medicine, and regenerative science. 
 
Additional projects have included: 
 Examining bioethical considerations associated with scientific research. 
 Exploring environmentally responsible methods of delivering medications. 
 Investigating sustainable packaging materials that could reduce waste. 
 Developing student-designed experiments based on questions and hypotheses. 
 Exploring how biological materials might be used to support tissue regeneration. 
 
Ms. Sheehan reported that a professor at Saint Anselm College expressed interest in establishing a 
partnership through which her students could assist with research involving mollusk tissues. 
The proposed research would explore whether these tissues could serve as scaffolds for growing 
biological structures, including ligaments and tendons.  She explained that partnerships established 
through Manchester Creates have created opportunities for students to participate in meaningful scientific 
investigations and connect with professionals conducting research in these fields. 
 
Ms. Sheehan reflected on how the experience had changed her approach to teaching. 
She explained that she has become more willing to encourage students to explore their own scientific 
questions and develop experiments rather than limiting classroom activities to predetermined 
investigations.  She emphasized the importance of allowing students to test ideas, evaluate results, and 
learn from both successful and unsuccessful experiments.  She also shared the personal significance of 
watching her daughter, Liz, develop an interest in science.  She explained that Liz had not previously 
considered science a particular area of interest but became highly engaged through hands-on learning 
opportunities. 
 
Ms. Sheehan described the experience of watching her daughter confidently present research before an 
audience of more than 200 researchers and scientists.  She expressed her hope that students throughout the 
Manchester School District would have similar opportunities to discover their interests, develop 
confidence, and recognize their academic potential.
October 27, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 13 of 54 
 
 
Expanding Opportunities Across Manchester Schools 
 
Ms. Hartigan-Demers reported that Manchester Creates had expanded through three cohorts, establishing 
participation among educators from Manchester's middle and high schools.  She explained that the 
relationships developed through the program have created opportunities for teachers to collaborate across 
school buildings and establish a more consistent approach to biotechnology and regenerative medicine 
instruction. 
 
The presenters emphasized that these partnerships could serve as the foundation for developing a science 
pathway that allows students to build upon their knowledge as they progress through grade levels. 
Ms. Sheehan explained that the grant supporting Manchester Creates was scheduled to conclude in April 
2027. 
 
Although the end of funding presented challenges, she indicated that efforts were underway to identify 
additional grant opportunities and explore ways to continue the initiative. 
 
The presenters discussed several potential next steps. 
 
Millyard on the Map — Assured Learning Experience 
 
Ms. Sheehan discussed a proposed assured learning experience tentatively titled Millyard on the Map. 
The initiative would connect Manchester students with local biotechnology and regenerative medicine 
professionals, industry partners, and the University of New Hampshire at Manchester. 
 
The proposed experience would: 
 Introduce students to biotechnology and regenerative medicine research occurring in Manchester. 
 Provide opportunities to meet industry professionals and explore career pathways. 
 Connect classroom science instruction with real-world applications. 
 Highlight Manchester's growing biotechnology industry. 
 Incorporate community connections and civic responsibility. 
 Encourage students to consider how scientific innovation contributes to the City's economic and 
educational future.
October 27, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 14 of 54 
 
 
 
A potential pilot involving approximately 150 students was being explored for April. 
 
The longer-term goal would be to expand participation to seventh- and tenth-grade students throughout 
the District. 
 
Ms. Sheehan expressed enthusiasm about the opportunity to connect students with local researchers and 
industry representatives and hoped that the initiative could eventually become available to all students at 
the identified grade levels. 
 
Future Biotechnology Coursework 
 
Ms. Sheehan discussed the possibility of expanding existing high school science coursework to include 
additional content related to biotechnology, regenerative medicine, and biofabrication.  She explained that 
the District already has some relevant course offerings that could potentially be updated or expanded. 
The presenters emphasized that partnerships with local colleges, universities, and biotechnology 
organizations could provide instructional resources and expertise to support these efforts. 
 
BioTrek and Middle School Science 
 
Ms. Hartigan-Demers discussed opportunities to expand biotechnology instruction at the middle school 
level through partnerships with the Advanced Regenerative Manufacturing Institute (ARMI).  She 
explained that Hillside Middle School currently participates in the BioTrek program and expressed 
interest in expanding similar opportunities to other middle schools.  She emphasized that introducing 
students to biotechnology earlier in their educational experience could strengthen science engagement and 
provide a foundation for more advanced coursework in high school. 
 
Interdisciplinary Frankenstein Project 
 
Ms. Hartigan-Demers described a planned interdisciplinary project connecting regenerative medicine with 
the study of Frankenstein in language arts.  Students would apply scientific concepts involving tissue
October 27, 2026, Teaching and Learning Agenda 
Page 15 of 54 
 
 
regeneration and biofabrication to examine how the fictional creature might be reconstructed using 
regenerative medicine. 
 
The project would incorporate: 
 Science and regenerative medicine. 
 Literature and language arts. 
 Critical thinking and problem-solving. 
 Creativity and scientific design. 
 Project-based learning and collaboration. 
 
Ms. Hartigan-Demers explained that the project would allow students to make connections between 
scientific research and literature while developing a greater understanding of emerging medical 
technologies.  She also discussed the possibility of presenting the project at the National Science 
Teaching Association conference in March, noting that a proposal had been submitted. 
Both presenters expressed enthusiasm about continuing their professional learning and potentially sharing 
their instructional experiences through future presentations or publications. 
 
Committee Members questions and comments included: 
 
1.  Committee Member Turner thanked the presenters and requested additional background 
regarding Manchester Creates and how the cohort model operates.  She explained that 
providing this information would be helpful for newer Committee members and members 
of the public who may be unfamiliar with the program. 
 
Ms. Sheehan explained that Manchester Creates was established through grant funding to provide 
educators with professional development, instructional materials, and ongoing support in biomedical 
engineering, biofabrication, and regenerative medicine.  The program was structured over three years, 
with different cohorts of participating teachers developing project-based learning experiences for their 
classrooms. 
 
Ms. Hartigan-Demers added that an important component was access to laboratory facilities at the 
University of New Hampshire at Manchester.  Teachers were able to learn laboratory procedures,

experiment with materials such as hydrogels, and develop hands-on scientific activities they could bring

professional support, was particularly valuable in helping teachers gain the confidence and skills 
necessary to introduce advanced scientific concepts. 
 
They expressed disappointment that the current grant was ending in April 2027 but indicated that efforts 
to secure additional funding were underway. 
 
2.  Committee Member Turner praised Manchester Creates for developing skills that extend 
beyond biotechnology, including collaboration, communication, data collection, critical 
thinking, experimentation, and problem-solving.  She emphasized that these are 
foundational scientific skills that benefit students regardless of the particular scientific field

3. Committee Member Turner expressed concern that innovative, hands-on science

importance of strengthening science instruction across all grade levels, particularly in 
middle school, where students can build upon the curiosity and foundational skills 
developed during elementary school.  She recalled her experience organizing science fairs 
and observing students develop confidence as they presented research projects, discussed 
their findings, and explained both the successes and challenges of their experiments. 
 
4. Committee Member Turner suggested that expanding project-based learning would 
require: 
 Continued professional development for science teachers. 
 Opportunities for educators to collaborate and share successful instructional practices. 
 Appropriate funding for laboratory materials and supplies. 
 Encouraging teachers to incorporate student-led investigations. 
 Strengthening the consistency and rigor of science instruction across schools.

Special Education Process and Timelines 
 
Mr. Roth reviewed the special education process, explaining that it begins with a referral and continues 
through evaluation, eligibility determination, development of an Individualized Education Program (IEP), 
and identification of an appropriate educational placement.  He outlined the timelines governing the 
process:

services and educational environments designed to meet individual student needs.  He emphasized that all 
students are general education students first and that the District strives to provide students with access to

Students may receive special education services in several settings:
